newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Veil lifting on S.Africa's cloak and dagger world.
newsitem.headline: Veil lifting on S.Africa's cloak and dagger world.

text.p: The arrest of South Africa's top expert in chemical and biological warfare promises to lift the veil on a cloak and dagger world of arms and drug smuggling.
Security chiefs said foreign agents were very interested in Brigadier Wouter Basson, arrested in Pretoria a month ago on drug dealing charges, who is out on bail but hiding in fear of his life.

"The man's a genius," deputy defence minister Ronnie Kasrils told a news conference on Thursday where he and defence force surgeon-general Lieutenant-General Daniel Knobel sought to answer criticism over the government's handling of Basson.
Basson -- who is a chemical scientist and heart surgeon -- led a project which began in the 1980s to develop defences against chemical and biological weapons.
He was given early retirement from the defence force in March 1993 by then-president F.W. de Klerk, who feared he had been involved in apartheid-era crimes.

Kasrils said that in the year following his retirement Basson had travelled widely, including to Libya, and that this had caused "tremendous concern" that he might be selling his chemical warfare knowledge.
As a result President Nelson Mandela's government rehired Basson after it took office in May 1994 so that it could keep a tighter rein on him.
"We had to prevent that wanderlust of his emerging all the time," Kasrils said.

A separate statement issued by Mandela's office on Thursday said the government had wanted Basson's position to be "appropriately regularised and regulated" as a way of preventing proliferation of South Africa's chemical warfare expertise.
Knobel said that after being rehired by the defence force, Basson cooperated in investigations into fraud cases associated with sanctions-busting arms deals during the apartheid years.
In one such case, $1.6 million of South African money had gone missing in Croatia during efforts to buy strategic chemicals, Knobel said.
He said that when police arrested Basson on the drugs charge, the scientist had initially believed Israeli agents were trying to abduct or kill him because of his links with Libya.

Basson is now being guarded at a secret location by members of South Africa's intelligence service but his lawyer has said he is willing to give public testimony to the Truth and Reconciliation Commission. The commission has yet to set a date for the hearing.
The Basson case has revived interest in a series of murders in South Africa in the early 1990s, at least one of which was said by police to have been carried out by the Israeli secret service Mossad.
Israel denied any involvement in the murder of Alan Kidger, who police said appeared to have been involved in smuggling strategic chemicals to the Middle East.
Kidger's family have said they would like the truth commission to set up a meeting between them and Basson in case he can throw any light on the still unsolved killing.
Security sources say that networks set up during the apartheid era to circumvent sanctions were later used for purely criminal ends like drug smuggling.
Knobel said South Africa had "begged, robbed and stolen" chemical weapons technology from East and West during the 1980s.

"Clearly the West would very much like to know what we know about Eastern technology, and the other way round," he said. "We've already made available some information on Eastern technology to the West with which they were very much impressed."
